abstract.shortdesc: Brief rundown of the elements you can use in topic type topics.

section.title: Structure Blocks
section.p: These are the elements that make up a topic.

dlentry.dd: The defining container
All topics need a title. Note that there is only one title element. All things that can use a title use this same element, whether that is a topic, section, figure, table, etc.

The short description for the topic. This is the first sentence of the topic. This element can be picked up in search results or when generating links.
Alternatively, you can use an abstract. The abstract allows for more content than a shortdesc, but it is not extracted and reused the same way. However, you can place multiple shortdesc inside an abstract, which can be useful when dealing with conditional content.

A place to put all the metadata for the topic. In general, nothing in this section emits in the topic. This can include:
Author
Source
Publisher
Copyright
Change History List (technically a specialization, but I'm listing all the prolog things here)
Critical Dates
Metadata: keywords, index terms, and 'other meta' such as any name value pair you need.
The container that holds the content of the topic
A list of links to other topics of interest (instead of having links in the text).

section.title: Body blocks
section.p: These are the elements that can be used as blocks inside of the body.
Technically, the topic should not contain specializations. However, the technical content components are usually just included with.

dlentry.dd: Generic container to group content. It can only be used inside of a body, so it's mainly for using for specialization.
This is a specialization from the programming domain, but it indicates multiple lines of code.

A generic container. It can group content with no semantic meaning. In general, avoid using, except for when grouping together a set of blocks you want to reuse instead of dealing with using the fancy conref attributes.

Definition list. You can provide a term and at least one definition. Super useful. Can be displayed as a funky formatted list or as a table. If you add an id attribute to the dlentry element, the dt is automagically returned in the xref.

Basic name value pair for specialization. Does not emit by default. In general, don't use except when you want to support funky processing without a specialization (if you know how to change the formatting).
Funky extension thing used with data. Used for specializations. Don't use.

One of my favorite elements. The DITA-OT includes a parameter that excludes this element. Enables you to include comments and questions in your writing with less fear that it will show up in the output.
To define where you're inserting an equation using mathml or just an image. Equations often need special formatting or funky fonts, so identifying them can be useful.
As equation-block, but you can add a title.
A specialized section that identifies the content as an example.
A grouping that identifies a figure. Generally, this is an image with a caption (title), but could contain text or a codeblock.
A special element for identifying things that aren't DITA. Available for specialization. Do not use.
Fancy specialized Hazard Statements for and .
How you link to an image.
A special image where you can identify zones in the image and associate links with those zones.
A block where white space is preserved, but not necessarily using monospaced font. Often used for addresses or poetry.
Long quote. When you want to identify a quotation that contains multiple paragraphs.
An element that can contain MATHML, an XML based language for rendering equations.
A special block for messages, usually from software.
A container for short(ish) content you want to emphasize in some way. The default DITA contains several types of notes, including tip, warning, caution, and important.
An element to reference something not-DITA, such as a video.
Ordered list, just like HTML.
A paragraph, just like HTML.
A parameter list. A special list, like dl, but for parameters. Not used very often.
Preformatted text, just like HTML.
Special element that you should only see during conversion work. If a conversion transform finds a lump of content it can't deal with, wrap it in required-cleanup and let a human deal with it.
A specialization to identify content you see on a screen. Very useful when dealing with command line content.
A division to group content with an optional title. In general, section titles are not included in the table of contents.
A basic table. In DITA 1.3, does not allow row or column spanning. You can only control whether or not separators display.
Simple list. Provides a list without bullets or numbering.
Special element meant to be used with indexes.
Special element if you want to include raw SVG code in your topic.
Super specialized element for syntax diagrams, used in some programming languages.
A CALS based table.
Unordered list. Same as HTML.
Element for specialization. Do not use.

section.title: Inline elements
section.p: There are many block elements that can be used inside of other block elements. For example, you can have an image or ul inside of a p. I am not including those elements again here.

I personally prefer keeping my elements separate. I do not like to have a list inside of a p, I prefer the list to be after the paragraph. This is my best practice. However other people prefer having the block items inside of paragraphs so that it's easier to reuse them together. That may have made more sense in earlier editions of DITA, but now that you can define conrefs to contain multiple elements, or use a div to combine them, I prefer to keep things as tidy as possible. Since a lot of formatting is either CSS or XSL-FO based, inheritance matters. A ul inside of a p may inherit different margins etc. that just makes troubleshooting formatting issues a pain.

dlentry.dd: Generic bold. Avoid if possible and pick something semantic.
Formatting to strike through content.
Generic identifier of some sort of mark up. Meant for specialization.
Formatting to have a line over the text.
Subscript - Use as needed.
Superscript - Use as needed.
Generic monospace formatting. Same as HTML. Try to use something semantic.
Generic underline formatting. Same as HTML. Try to use something semantic.
If you use all the special bits of glossaries and the abbreviation domain, use this to identify the abbreviated form of a term.
For API names
To identify a citation.
A command name.
A code phrase
Like equation-block, but you can have your math inline.
For paths when describing things on computers.
Footnote. You enter it right in the text, and the processing will put it at the bottom of the page.
If you need to have index terms in your content, you can put them where needed, not just in the prolog
If you need to do any of that "see also" stuff in your index.
Identifies an important word. Generally has no formatting, but can help with search results if your processing supports it. Also useful for rendering keys of simple phrases.
In the software world, you constantly need to identify a set of nested options in menus. Use the menucascade to identify and format them for you. For example: Select File Open .
If your system provides codes or IDs for system messages, use this to identify it.
For inline system messages.
XML Domain to identify when you reference funky characters by Hex codes. For example Ώ is x38f.
For software or programming, an option.
XML Domain for parameter entities in schemas.
For software or programming, a parameter name.
A phrase. No semantic meaning or formatting, but crazy useful for inserting keys or marking sentences for conditions.
An inline quote.
Syntax phrase. Similar to codeph, but slightly different. Sorta like syntax is an algebra equation a + b = c but codeph is a math equation 1 + 2 = 3.
Response from a system.
Identifies something as a word of importance. You can hook it up with keys to a glossary entry to link to the definition.
XML domain to identify text entities in schemas.
Use to identify something as a trademark. For example Soon.
Something in the user interface.
User input, i.e. something you type in.
Variable name
Window title. Can be used for a window, screen, dialog box, etc.
XML domain attribute name
XML Domain element name
XML Domain name space
XML Domain processing instruction
How you define links.
Meant for specialization, an element that can be true or false. Do not use.
A name value pair for specialization. Do not use.
Mainly intended as a specialization element. Avoid using.
